claim: BST2/tetherin is an antiviral restriction factor that inhibits the release of enveloped viruses from the cell surface.
source: BST2/tetherin, an antiviral restriction factor, inhibits the release of enveloped viruses from the cell surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Neil et al., 2008; Van Damme et al., 2008; Jouvenet et al., 2009; Evans et al., 2010; Arias et al., 2012) as referenced in the Introduction.

claim: HIV-1 antagonizes BST2 through viral protein u (Vpu), which downregulates BST2 from the cell surface.
source: Human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) antagonizes BST2 through viral protein u (Vpu), which downregulates BST2 from the cell surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Neil et al., 2008; Van Damme et al., 2008) as referenced in the Introduction.

claim: The crystal structure of a protein complex containing Vpu and BST2 cytoplasmic domains and the core of AP1 was determined.
source: We report the crystal structure of a protein complex containing Vpu and BST2 cytoplasmic domains and the core of the clathrin adaptor protein complex 1 (AP1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including crystallographic data collection and refinement statistics in Table 1 and structural figures (Figure 5).

claim: Vpu mimics a canonical acidic dileucine-sorting motif to bind AP1 in the cytosol.
source: Vpu mimics a canonical acidic dileucine-sorting motif to bind AP1 in the cytosol, while simultaneously interacting with BST2 in the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data showing the Vpu ELV motif binding to the acidic dileucine-binding site of AP1 (Figure 5F, G).

claim: Vpu simultaneously interacts with BST2 in the membrane while binding AP1.
source: Vpu mimics a canonical acidic dileucine-sorting motif to bind AP1 in the cytosol, while simultaneously interacting with BST2 in the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure showing BST2 and Vpu binding to different sites on AP1 (Figure 5A), and by prior work on transmembrane interactions (Mangeat et al., 2009; Skasko et al., 2012; McNatt et al., 2009; Vigan and Neil, 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2011; Vigan and Neil, 2010).

claim: Vpu builds on an intrinsic interaction between BST2 and AP1.
source: These interactions enable Vpu to build on an intrinsic interaction between BST2 and AP1, presumably causing the observed retention of BST2 in juxtanuclear endosomes and stimulating its degradation in lysosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro binding data showing BST2 binds μ1 of AP1 (Figure 1A), and by the crystal structure showing both BST2 and Vpu binding to AP1 (Figure 5A).

claim: Vpu causes retention of BST2 in juxtanuclear endosomes.
source: These interactions enable Vpu to build on an intrinsic interaction between BST2 and AP1, presumably causing the observed retention of BST2 in juxtanuclear endosomes and stimulating its degradation in lysosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing co-localization of BST2, Vpu, and AP1 at the cell center (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 1), and by citations to prior work (Douglas et al., 2009; Dube et al., 2010; Hauser et al., 2010; Lau et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011).

claim: Vpu stimulates degradation of BST2 in lysosomes.
source: These interactions enable Vpu to build on an intrinsic interaction between BST2 and AP1, presumably causing the observed retention of BST2 in juxtanuclear endosomes and stimulating its degradation in lysosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on BST2 degradation pathways (Van Damme et al., 2008; Douglas et al., 2009; Goffinet et al., 2009; Iwabu et al., 2009; Mangeat et al., 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Janvier et al., 2011) and by functional data showing decreased BST2 expression with wild-type Vpu (Figure 7F, Figure 8B).

claim: BST2 has a short cytoplasmic tail at the N-terminus followed by a single transmembrane helix, a long coiled-coil extracellular domain, and a C-terminal GPI anchor.
source: BST2 has a short cytoplasmic tail at the N-terminus followed by a single transmembrane (TM) helix, a long coiled-coil extracellular domain, and a C-terminal glycosyl phosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor (Kupzig et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Kupzig et al., 2003).

claim: The availability of two membrane anchors connected by a long coiled-coil allows BST2 to efficiently inhibit viral transmission by tethering newly formed virions at the infected cell surface.
source: The availability of two membrane anchors connected by a long coiled-coil allows BST2 to efficiently inhibit viral transmission by tethering newly formed virions at the infected cell surface and preventing their release to the surrounding environment (Hinz et al., 2010; Schubert et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hinz et al., 2010; Schubert et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2010).

claim: The short intracellular, N-terminal tail of BST2 has been implicated in the natural trafficking of this antiviral protein.
source: The short intracellular, N-terminal tail of BST2 has been implicated in the natural trafficking of this antiviral protein (Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).

claim: Vpu associates with BST2 through an anti-parallel interaction between the transmembrane domains of each protein.
source: Vpu associates with BST2 through an anti-parallel interaction between the transmembrane domains of each protein (Mangeat et al., 2009; Skasko et al., 2012; McNatt et al., 2009; Vigan and Neil, 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2011; Vigan and Neil, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mangeat et al., 2009; Skasko et al., 2012; McNatt et al., 2009; Vigan and Neil, 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2011; Vigan and Neil, 2010).

claim: The transmembrane interaction between Vpu and BST2 is species-specific and essential for the antagonism of BST2 by Vpu.
source: This interaction is species-specific and essential for the antagonism of BST2 by Vpu (McNatt et al., 2009; Skasko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (McNatt et al., 2009; Skasko et al., 2012).

claim: Part of Vpu's activity against BST2 can be explained by the viral hijacking of the β-TrCP-associated ubiquitin–proteasome degradation pathway.
source: Part of Vpu's activity against BST2 can be explained by the viral hijacking of the β-TrCP-associated ubiquitin–proteasome degradation pathway (Van Damme et al., 2008; Douglas et al., 2009; Goffinet et al., 2009; Iwabu et al., 2009; Mangeat et al., 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Van Damme et al., 2008; Douglas et al., 2009; Goffinet et al., 2009; Iwabu et al., 2009; Mangeat et al., 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009).

claim: HRS, a component of the ESCRT-0 machinery, has been suggested to recognize ubiquitinated BST2 and target it for lysosomal degradation.
source: A component of the ESCRT-0 machinery, HRS, has also been suggested to recognize ubiquitinated BST2 and target it for lysosomal degradation (Janvier et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Janvier et al., 2011).

claim: Degradation pathways are only partially responsible for the antagonism of BST2 by Vpu.
source: However, these degradation pathways are only partially responsible for the antagonism of BST2 by Vpu (Van Damme et al., 2008; Douglas et al., 2009; Iwabu et al., 2009; Mangeat et al., 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Van Damme et al., 2008; Douglas et al., 2009; Iwabu et al., 2009; Mangeat et al., 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009).

claim: Efficient BST2 downregulation from the cell surface can occur in the absence of BST2 degradation.
source: Efficient BST2 downregulation from the cell surface can occur in the absence of BST2 degradation (Dube et al., 2010; Goffinet et al., 2010; Tervo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Dube et al., 2010; Goffinet et al., 2010; Tervo et al., 2011).

claim: Vpu induces the mistrafficking of BST2, causing the accumulation of BST2 at the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
source: Moreover, Vpu induces the mistrafficking of BST2 (Douglas et al., 2009; Dube et al., 2010; Hauser et al., 2010; Lau et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011), causing the accumulation of BST2 at the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Douglas et al., 2009; Dube et al., 2010; Hauser et al., 2010; Lau et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011).

claim: Both recycled and newly synthesized BST2 are retained at the TGN, blocking the resupply of BST2 to the plasma membrane and eventually leading to its depletion at the cell surface.
source: Both recycled and newly synthesized BST2 are retained at the TGN, blocking the resupply of BST2 to the plasma membrane and eventually leading to its depletion at the cell surface (Dube et al., 2011; Lau et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Dube et al., 2011; Lau et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011).

claim: Mutations in the juxta-membrane hinge region of Vpu that interfere with the localization of Vpu to the TGN impair the antagonism of BST2.
source: Moreover, mutations in the juxta-membrane hinge region of Vpu that interfere with the localization of Vpu to the TGN impair the antagonism of BST2 (Dube et al., 2009; Vigan and Neil, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Dube et al., 2009; Vigan and Neil, 2011).

claim: Clathrin-dependent trafficking pathways have been suggested to be involved in the Vpu-mediated mistrafficking of BST2.
source: Clathrin-dependent trafficking pathways have been suggested to be involved in the Vpu-mediated mistrafficking of BST2 (Kueck and Neil, 2012; Lau et al., 2011; Mitchell et al., 2009; Ruiz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kueck and Neil, 2012; Lau et al., 2011; Mitchell et al., 2009; Ruiz et al., 2008).

claim: Clathrin-dependent trafficking pathways regulate the trafficking of cellular membrane proteins by selectively packaging these membrane cargos into clathrin-coated vesicles (CCV).
source: Such pathways regulate the trafficking of cellular membrane proteins by selectively packaging these membrane cargos into clathrin-coated vesicles (CCV) (Bonifacino and Traub, 2003; Canagarajah et al., 2013; Traub, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Bonifacino and Traub, 2003; Canagarajah et al., 2013; Traub, 2009).

claim: The clathrin adaptor protein (AP) complexes mediate cargo selection in clathrin-dependent trafficking pathways.
source: The clathrin adaptor protein (AP) complexes mediate this cargo selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about AP complexes and their role in cargo selection.

claim: Two canonical sorting motifs in the cytoplasmic domains of membrane cargo proteins are recognized by the AP complexes: a tyrosine-based Yxxϕ motif and an acidic dileucine motif, [E/D]xxxL[L/I].
source: Two canonical sorting motifs in the cytoplasmic domains of the membrane cargo proteins are recognized by the AP complexes: a tyrosine-based Yxxϕ motif (ϕ represents a large hydrophobic residue; x for any amino acid) and an acidic dileucine motif, [E/D]xxxL[L/I].
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about AP complex recognition motifs.

claim: Five AP complexes exist in the cell and each is responsible for trafficking by distinct routes.
source: Five AP complexes exist in the cell and each is responsible for trafficking by distinct routes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about AP complexes.

claim: AP1 traffics cargo between the TGN and sorting endosomes.
source: For example, AP1 traffics cargo between the TGN and sorting endosomes, while AP2 selects cargo for transport between the plasma membrane and early endosomes (Canagarajah et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Canagarajah et al., 2013) and established scientific knowledge.

claim: AP2 selects cargo for transport between the plasma membrane and early endosomes.
source: For example, AP1 traffics cargo between the TGN and sorting endosomes, while AP2 selects cargo for transport between the plasma membrane and early endosomes (Canagarajah et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Canagarajah et al., 2013) and established scientific knowledge.

claim: In the absence of Vpu, the natural trafficking of endogenous BST2 depends on the clathrin-associated pathways.
source: In the absence of Vpu, the natural trafficking of endogenous BST2 depends on the clathrin-associated pathways, and the involvement of both AP1 and AP2 has been suggested (Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).

claim: The involvement of both AP1 and AP2 in BST2 trafficking has been suggested.
source: In the absence of Vpu, the natural trafficking of endogenous BST2 depends on the clathrin-associated pathways, and the involvement of both AP1 and AP2 has been suggested (Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).

claim: An unusual double-tyrosine motif, YxY, in the BST2 cytoplasmic domain (BST2CD) is critical for the natural trafficking of BST2.
source: An unusual double-tyrosine motif, YxY, in the BST2 cytoplasmic domain (BST2CD) is critical for this natural trafficking (Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).

claim: A putative clathrin-sorting motif, ExxxLV (ELV), located in the membrane-distal half of Vpu's cytoplasmic domain (VpuCD) was shown to be important for BST2 antagonism.
source: In Vpu, a putative clathrin-sorting motif, ExxxLV (ELV), located in the membrane-distal half of the protein's cytoplasmic domain (VpuCD) was shown to be important for BST2 antagonism (Kueck and Neil, 2012, McNatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kueck and Neil, 2012, McNatt et al., 2013).

claim: Vpu-induced virion release and removal of BST2 from the cell surface are inhibited by a dominant negative mutant of AP180.
source: Furthermore, Vpu-induced virion release and removal of BST2 from the cell surface are inhibited by a dominant negative mutant of AP180, a protein required for the assembly of the CCV at the lipid membrane (Kueck and Neil, 2012; Lau et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kueck and Neil, 2012; Lau et al., 2011).

claim: BST2CD specifically binds μ1 of AP1, but not μ2 of AP2 or μ3 of AP3.
source: BST2 specifically binds μ1 of AP1, but not μ2 of AP2 or μ3 of AP3
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data (Figure 1A-C) and yeast two-hybrid assays (Figure 1D).

claim: The purified μ1-CTD of AP1 bound BST2CD as the two co-migrated as a higher molecular weight complex on a size exclusion column.
source: The purified μ1-CTD of AP1 bound BST2CD as the two co-migrated as a higher molecular weight complex on a size exclusion column (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No binding was observed between BST2CD and either the μ2-CTD or μ3-CTD.
source: In contrast, no such binding was observed for either the μ2-CTD (Figure 1B) or μ3-CTD (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: BST2CD exhibited binding to μ1, but not μ2 or μ3, in the yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Consistent with the in vitro binding assay, BST2CD exhibited binding to μ1, but not μ2 or μ3, in the Y2H assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The TGN38 peptide containing a canonical YxxΦ motif displayed binding to all three μ subunits (μ1, μ2, and μ3).
source: As controls, the TGN38 peptide containing a canonical YxxΦ motif displayed binding to all three μ subunits, and a mutant μ1 subunit (μ1 D174A) with a disrupted binding pocket for tyrosine-based motifs bound neither TGN38 nor the BST2CD.
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A mutant μ1 subunit (μ1 D174A) with a disrupted binding pocket for tyrosine-based motifs bound neither TGN38 nor the BST2CD.
source: As controls, the TGN38 peptide containing a canonical YxxΦ motif displayed binding to all three μ subunits, and a mutant μ1 subunit (μ1 D174A) with a disrupted binding pocket for tyrosine-based motifs bound neither TGN38 nor the BST2CD.
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The binding between BST2CD and μ1 was abolished by the double alanine mutation of the YxY motif (Y6/8A) in BST2CD.
source: Furthermore, this binding was abolished by the double alanine mutation of the YxY motif (Y6/8A) in BST2CD.
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: BST2CD contains a tyrosine-based motif to allow for AP binding and a specificity determinant to select specifically for μ1.
source: These results indicate that BST2CD not only contains a tyrosine-based motif to allow for AP binding, but also a specificity determinant to select specifically for μ1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing selective binding of BST2CD to μ1 but not μ2 or μ3 (Figure 1).

claim: BST2 binds to the μ1 subunit of AP1, but not μ2 of AP2.
source: Our results support the involvement of AP1 in trafficking of BST2 and are consistent with a previous observation that BST2 binds to the μ1 subunit of AP1, but not μ2 of AP2 (Masuyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' data (Figure 1) and citation to prior work (Masuyama et al., 2009).

claim: In the absence of Vpu, BST2 has been suggested to localize to the TGN through clathrin-dependent trafficking.
source: In the absence of Vpu, BST2 has been suggested to localize to the TGN through clathrin-dependent trafficking (Kupzig et al., 2003; Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009), and the BST2–AP1 interaction may be responsible for this localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kupzig et al., 2003; Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009).

claim: The BST2–AP1 interaction may be responsible for BST2 localization to the TGN.
source: In the absence of Vpu, BST2 has been suggested to localize to the TGN through clathrin-dependent trafficking (Kupzig et al., 2003; Rollason et al., 2007; Masuyama et al., 2009), and the BST2–AP1 interaction may be responsible for this localization.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed BST2-AP1 interaction and prior work on BST2 localization.

claim: An involvement of AP2 in BST2 trafficking has been suggested to occur through its α appendage domain.
source: In contrast, an involvement of AP2 in BST2 trafficking has been suggested to occur through its α appendage domain.
evidence: This claim is based on prior suggestions in the literature, though the authors' data did not detect this interaction.

claim: The interaction between BST2 and the α appendage domain of AP2 was not detected in the in vitro binding test using size exclusion chromatography.
source: However, this interaction was not detected in our in vitro binding test using size exclusion chromatography (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MBP-VpuCD co-migrated with the μ1-truncated AP1 as a complex on a size exclusion column.
source: Indeed, MBP-VpuCD co-migrated with the μ1-truncated AP1 as a complex on a size exclusion column (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The binding between VpuCD and μ1-truncated AP1 was abolished by the alanine-mutation of the ELV motif.
source: Importantly, the binding was abolished by the alanine-mutation of the ELV motif, signifying the crucial role of the ELV motif in the interaction between Vpu and AP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The ELV motif plays a crucial role in the interaction between Vpu and AP1.
source: Importantly, the binding was abolished by the alanine-mutation of the ELV motif, signifying the crucial role of the ELV motif in the interaction between Vpu and AP1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that mutation of the ELV motif abolishes binding (Figure 2B).

claim: Binding between VpuCD and μ1-CTD was observed using size exclusion chromatography.
source: We further tested the binding between VpuCD and μ1-CTD and observed complex formation using size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Vpu has evolved the ability to associate with multiple subunits of AP1.
source: These interactions demonstrate that Vpu has evolved the ability to associate with multiple subunits of AP1, potentially allowing it to modulate the cellular trafficking machinery to target host proteins such as BST2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing Vpu binding to different AP1 subunits (Figure 2A-C).

claim: Vpu can potentially modulate the cellular trafficking machinery to target host proteins such as BST2.
source: These interactions demonstrate that Vpu has evolved the ability to associate with multiple subunits of AP1, potentially allowing it to modulate the cellular trafficking machinery to target host proteins such as BST2.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed Vpu-AP1 interactions.

claim: VpuCD binds to the truncated hemicomplex of AP2, α (1–398)-σ.
source: We used size exclusion chromatography to test the binding between VpuCD and a truncated hemicomplex of AP2, α (1–398)-σ, which contains the binding pocket for the acidic dileucine sorting motif; an interaction complex was observed (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Binding between VpuCD and the μ2-CTD of AP2 was observed.
source: Furthermore, binding between VpuCD and the μ2-CTD of AP2 was also observed (Figure 2E), while no such binding was observed between VpuCD and the μ3-CTD of AP3 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No binding was observed between VpuCD and the μ3-CTD of AP3.
source: Furthermore, binding between VpuCD and the μ2-CTD of AP2 was also observed (Figure 2E), while no such binding was observed between VpuCD and the μ3-CTD of AP3 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Vpu specifically interacts with AP1 and AP2, which may allow the viral protein to hijack the associated trafficking pathways.
source: Altogether, these results suggest specific interactions between Vpu and AP1 and AP2, which may allow the viral protein to hijack the associated trafficking pathways.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing Vpu binding to AP1 and AP2 but not AP3 (Figure 2).

claim: Vpu does not increase the rate of BST2 internalization from the cell surface, with one exception.
source: This notion is supported by multiple observations, with one exception (Iwabu et al., 2010), that Vpu does not increase the rate of BST2 internalization from the cell surface (Mitchell et al., 2009; Dube et al., 2010; Andrew et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mitchell et al., 2009; Dube et al., 2010; Andrew et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011), with one exception noted (Iwabu et al., 2010).

claim: The fusion protein BST2CD-VpuCD exhibited strong binding to the GST-tagged AP1 in the pulldown assay.
source: The fusion protein exhibited strong binding to the GST-tagged AP1 in the pulldown assay (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Individual interactions of VpuCD and BST2CD with the full AP1 core complex were not observed under stringent pulldown conditions.
source: In contrast, although both VpuCD and BST2CD interact with AP1 subunits in our size exclusion chromatography assays (Figure 1, Figure 2), their individual interactions with the full AP1 core complex were not observed under stringent pulldown conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An additive or cooperative effect occurs when BST2CD and VpuCD bind to AP1.
source: This result suggests that an additive or cooperative effect occurs when BST2CD and VpuCD bind to AP1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the fusion protein binds AP1 strongly while individual domains do not (Figure 3B).

claim: Alanine mutation of the YxY motif (Y6/8A) greatly reduced the binding of BST2CD-VpuCD fusion to AP1.
source: As expected, alanine mutation of the YxY motif (Y6/8A) greatly reduced the binding to AP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Additional mutation of the γ subunit R15E on AP1 that disrupts the acidic dileucine-motif binding site further affected the binding.
source: Additional mutation of the γ subunit R15E on AP1 that disrupts the acidic dileucine-motif binding site affected the binding further.
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Binding between endogenous AP1 (the µ1 subunit) and the BST2-Vpu chimera was detected.
source: Consistent with the in vitro observations (Figure 3B), binding between endogenous AP1 (the µ1subunit) and this chimera was detected, while no such binding was detected for either BST2 or Vpu alone (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No binding between endogenous AP1 and either BST2 or Vpu alone was detected in the immunoprecipitation experiment.
source: Consistent with the in vitro observations (Figure 3B), binding between endogenous AP1 (the µ1subunit) and this chimera was detected, while no such binding was detected for either BST2 or Vpu alone (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mutant combining both Y6/8A and ELV/AAA mutations was unable to bind AP1.
source: Although the alanine mutations of either Y6/8 or ELV did not substantially reduce the binding, the mutant combining both sets of mutations was unable to bind AP1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The binding of Vpu to AP1 is independent of serine-phosphorylation.
source: Our experiments show that the binding of Vpu to AP1 is independent of serine-phosphorylation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The unphosphorylated BST2CD-VpuCD fusion protein bound AP1 as tightly as the phosphorylated construct.
source: The unphosphorylated fusion protein bound AP1 as tightly as the phosphorylated construct (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The binding of AP1 was not affected by the double mutation, S52/56N, that destroys the phosphorylation sites.
source: Furthermore, the binding of AP1 was not affected by the double mutation, S52/56N, that destroys the phosphorylation sites (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The β-TrCP-dependent BST2-degradation by Vpu and the mistrafficking of BST2 by Vpu are governed by different determinants in the VpuCD.
source: These results are consistent with the notion that the β-TrCP-dependent BST2-degradation by Vpu and the mistrafficking of BST2 by Vpu are governed by different determinants in the VpuCD.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that phosphorylation (required for β-TrCP binding) is not required for AP1 binding (Figure 4A).

claim: The crystal structure of the BST2CD-VpuCD fusion in complex with the AP1 core was determined at 3.0 Å resolution.
source: To understand the Vpu-enhanced binding of BST2 to AP1, we determined the crystal structure of the BST2CD-VpuCD fusion in complex with the AP1 core at 3.0 Å resolution (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1 and Figure 5A.

claim: The AP1 core adopts an activated, open conformation in the crystal structure, with both of its cargo binding sites exposed for interaction with BST2CD-VpuCD.
source: The AP1 core adopts an activated, open conformation, with both of its cargo binding sites exposed for interaction with BST2CD-VpuCD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The AP1 in the current structure adopts an open conformation distinct from that observed previously for AP2 and AP1.
source: The AP1 in the current structure adopts an open conformation distinct from that observed previously for AP2 and AP1 (Jackson et al., 2010; Ren et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current structure with previously published structures (Jackson et al., 2010; Ren et al., 2013), as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: BST2CD binds to the tyrosine motif-binding site on AP1 through critical interactions involving the YxY motif.
source: BST2CD binds to the tyrosine motif-binding site on AP1 through critical interactions involving the YxY motif, while VpuCD occupies the acidic dileucine motif-binding site of AP1 through the ELV motif.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: VpuCD occupies the acidic dileucine motif-binding site of AP1 through the ELV motif.
source: BST2CD binds to the tyrosine motif-binding site on AP1 through critical interactions involving the YxY motif, while VpuCD occupies the acidic dileucine motif-binding site of AP1 through the ELV motif.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A, F, G.

claim: Only a short region of VpuCD flanking the ELV motif is well ordered and successfully built in the structure.
source: Only a short region of VpuCD flanking the ELV motif is well ordered and successfully built in the structure.
evidence: This claim is based on the structural data and model building process.

claim: There is no direct interaction between BST2CD and VpuCD in the crystal structure.
source: There is no direct interaction between BST2CD and VpuCD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Vpu acts as an adaptor to increase the affinity of AP1 for BST2 by combining the viral protein's affinity for AP1 via the ELV motif and the tight transmembrane interaction with the host protein.
source: Overall, the structure reveals how Vpu enhances the native interaction between BST2 and AP1. claim: The binding mode for the three-component complex involving BST2, Vpu and AP1 is different from Nef/MHC-I/AP1, with no three-protein interface.
source: The binding mode for the three-component complex involving BST2, Vpu and AP1, is different, with no three-protein interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure showing separate binding sites for BST2 and Vpu on AP1 (Figure 5A, Figure 10A).

claim: The BST2/Vpu/AP1 complex is stabilized by pair-wise binary interactions: BST2 and Vpu bind through the transmembrane regions, BST2CD binds the AP1 μ1 subunit, and VpuCD binds the AP1 σ1/γ/μ1 subunits.
source: The complex is instead stabilized by pair-wise binary interactions: BST2 and Vpu bind through the transmembrane regions, BST2CD binds the AP1 μ1 subunit, and VpuCD binds the AP1 σ1/γ/μ1 subunits (Figure 10A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The BST2/Vpu/AP1 interaction model is consistent with previous findings that the transmembrane interaction between BST2 and Vpu is of pivotal importance in determining the activity of Vpu against BST2.
source: This model is consistent with the previous findings that the transmembrane interaction between BST2 and Vpu is of pivotal importance in determining the activity of Vpu against BST2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the current data and prior work on transmembrane interactions.

claim: The BST2/Vpu/AP1 interaction causes an open conformation of AP1 that has not been observed before.
source: The BST2/Vpu/AP1 interaction also causes an open conformation of AP1 that has not been observed before.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure showing a novel AP1 conformation (Figure 6A).

claim: This new AP1 conformation might only be induced by Vpu or alternatively it might exist as a physiologically functional state that Vpu selectively uses to its advantage.
source: This new AP1 conformation might only be induced by Vpu or alternatively it might exist as a physiologically functional state that Vpu selectively uses to its advantage.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of the novel AP1 conformation.

claim: The Vpu-mediated antagonism of BST2 appears to be a multifaceted process involving both AP1-mediated mistrafficking and degradation, and β-TrCP-mediated ubiquitination and the ESCRT machinery.
source: The Vpu-mediated antagonism of BST2 appears to be a multifaceted process. Besides AP1-mediated mistrafficking and degradation, Vpu can also induce the degradation of BST2 through β-TrCP-mediated ubiquitination and the ESCRT machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and citations to prior work.

claim: Abolishing either the ubiquitination pathway by the S52/56N mutation in Vpu or the mistrafficking pathway by the ELV/AAA mutation each led to defects in the enhancement of virion release.
source: Abolishing either the ubiquitination pathway by the S52/56N mutation in Vpu or the mistrafficking pathway by the ELV/AAA mutation each led to defects in the enhancement of virion release (Figure 8) (Kueck and Neil, 2012; McNatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by virion release assay data shown in Figure 8 and citations to prior work (Kueck and Neil, 2012; McNatt et al., 2013).

claim: Combining the S52/56N and ELV/AAA mutations caused the most substantial loss of Vpu function, suggesting a potentially parallel nature for these pathways.
source: Combining the two sets of mutations, however, appeared to cause the most substantial loss of Vpu function, suggesting a potentially parallel nature for these pathways.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the virion release assay data showing additive effects of the mutations (Figure 8).

claim: The complexity of trafficking and degradation mechanisms may have prevented a clear identification of the AP complex(es) responsible for the Vpu-activity in previous studies.
source: The complexity of these trafficking and degradation mechanisms may have prevented a clear identification of the AP complex(es) responsible for the Vpu-activity in previous studies (Kueck and Neil, 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the complexity of the system and citation to prior work (Kueck and Neil, 2012).

claim: Neither AP1, 2 or 3 knockdown in 293T cells and HeLa cells nor AP1 γ knockout in mouse fibroblasts had any apparent effects on the ability of Vpu to antagonize restriction by BST2.
source: Despite the evidence supporting the involvement of clathrin-associated pathways, neither AP1, 2 or 3 knockdown in 293T cells and HeLa cells nor AP1 γ knockout in mouse fibroblasts had any apparent effects on the ability of Vpu to antagonize restriction by BST2 (Kueck and Neil, 2012), although we previously reported a role for AP2 in the Vpu-mediated surface-downregulation of BST2 (Mitchell et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kueck and Neil, 2012; Mitchell et al., 2009).

claim: The individual roles of a given pathway may be obscured by compensation from overlapping parallel pathways, such as the involvement of multiple AP complexes or the monomeric clathrin adaptor HRS.
source: Conceivably, the individual roles of a given pathway are obscured by compensation from overlapping parallel pathways, such as the involvement of multiple AP complexes or the monomeric clathrin adaptor HRS.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference about potential compensatory mechanisms.

claim: Redundancy in the composition of an individual AP complex is possible, where a specific subunit of AP could be knocked down or out only to be replaced by a different isoform.
source: Another possibility is redundancy in the composition of an individual AP complex. A specific subunit of AP could be knocked down or out only to be replaced by a different isoform (Boehm and Bonifacino, 2001).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citation to prior work (Boehm and Bonifacino, 2001).

claim: Substitution might happen between two related subunits from different AP complexes as they have highly conserved structures.
source: Substitution might also happen between two related subunits from different AP complexes as they have highly conserved structures (Keyel et al., 2008; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citations to prior work (Keyel et al., 2008; Li et al., 2010).

claim: The mechanism of Vpu activity might be at least partly cell-type dependent.
source: Another level of complexity might come from the potential for the mechanism of Vpu activity to be at least partly cell-type dependent.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from observed differences in different cell types.

claim: In some cell types, BST2 appears to be equally vulnerable to β-TrCP-dependent degradation and to mistrafficking, whereas in others the role of β-TrCP-dependent degradation is less important, possibly due to lower levels of BST2 expression.
source: For example, BST2 in some cell types appears to be equally vulnerable to β-TrCP-dependent degradation and to mistrafficking, whereas in others the role of β-TrCP-dependent degradation is less important, possibly due to lower levels of BST2 expression (Schindler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Schindler et al., 2010).

claim: The intrinsic, structural flexibility of Vpu may enable its functional versatility and underlie the complexity of BST2-antagonism.
source: The intrinsic, structural flexibility of Vpu may enable its functional versatility and underlie the complexity of BST2-antagonism.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the structural data showing flexibility of VpuCD.

claim: A shared feature of retroviral accessory proteins including Vpu, Nef, Vif, Vpr and Vpx is the presence of long and flexible loops that provide the structural basis for their multifunctional nature.
source: A shared feature of retroviral accessory proteins including Vpu, Nef, Vif, Vpr and Vpx is the presence of long and flexible loops that provide the structural basis for their multifunctional nature (Xue et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Xue et al., 2012).

claim: Unstructured regions in retroviral accessory proteins can adopt different conformations to facilitate binding to different host target proteins.
source: These unstructured regions can adopt different conformations to facilitate binding to different host target proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about protein flexibility and binding.

claim: Unstructured regions in retroviral accessory proteins often harbor motifs mimicking functional host sequences, enabling the virus to hijack the desired host machineries.
source: These regions often harbor motifs mimicking functional host sequences, enabling the virus to hijack the desired host machineries (Kadaveru et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Kadaveru et al., 2008).

claim: The binding of the Vpu ELV motif to AP1 and the di-phosphoserine motif of Vpu to β-TrCP serve as two excellent examples of viral strategy to mimic host sequences.
source: The binding of the Vpu ELV motif to AP1 revealed in our structure, as well as that of the di-phosphoserine motif of Vpu to β-TrCP shown before, serve as two excellent examples of this viral strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current structural data and prior work on Vpu-β-TrCP interaction.

claim: The ExxxLV motif is conserved in the Vpu of subtype B of group M HIV-1.
source: The ExxxLV motif is conserved in the Vpu of subtype B of group M HIV-1, to which both NL4-3 and HV1S1 strains of HIV-1 used in this study belong.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of HIV-1 subtypes.

claim: In the Vpu sequence from the subtype C of the group M HIV-1, the ExxxLV motif is replaced by the consensus sequence ExxxMV.
source: However, in the Vpu sequence from the subtype C of the group M HIV-1, the motif is replaced by the consensus sequence ExxxMV, which might or might not be functionally equivalent to the ExxxLV sequence.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of HIV-1 subtypes.

claim: Subtype B Vpu localizes predominantly within internal membrane compartments, while subtype C Vpu is substantially expressed at the cell surface.
source: Interestingly, while subtype B Vpu localizes predominantly within internal membrane compartments, subtype C Vpu is substantially expressed at the cell surface (Pacyniak et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pacyniak et al., 2005).

claim: Subtype C Vpu contains another putative acidic dileucine motif in the membrane-proximal region of its CD, mutation of which affected the trafficking of Vpu.
source: In addition to the sequence variation in the ELV region, subtype C Vpu contains another putative acidic dileucine motif in the membrane-proximal region of its CD, mutation of which affected the trafficking of Vpu (Ruiz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ruiz et al., 2008).

claim: Subtype C Vpu may hijack AP complexes using residues distinct or partly overlapping with those used by subtype B Vpu.
source: Conceivably, subtype C Vpu hijacks AP complexes using residues distinct or partly overlapping with those used by subtype B Vpu.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from sequence differences between subtypes.

claim: The intrinsic affinity of Vpu to AP1 and AP2 suggests that Vpu has the ability to hijack clathrin-dependent trafficking pathways to target other cellular proteins with which it interacts simultaneously.
source: The intrinsic affinity of Vpu to AP1 and AP2 suggests that Vpu has the ability to hijack clathrin-dependent trafficking pathways to target other cellular proteins with which it interacts simultaneously.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed Vpu-AP interactions.

claim: HIV-1 Vpu modulates the surface expression of NTB-A and CD1d, in addition to BST2 and CD4.
source: Besides BST2 and CD4, HIV-1 Vpu also modulates the surface expression of two other important immune factors, NTB-A and CD1d (Sandberg et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sandberg et al., 2012).

claim: NTB-A is a co-activator for natural killer (NK) cells, and the Vpu induced downregulation of NTB-A enables infected cells to evade lysis by NK cells.
source: NTB-A is a co-activator for natural killer (NK) cells, and the Vpu induced downregulation of NTB-A enables infected cells to evade lysis by NK cells (Shah et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Shah et al., 2010).

claim: Vpu-mediated NTB-A downregulation involves the mistrafficking of NTB-A, which phenotypically resembles Vpu-mediated BST2 mistrafficking.
source: This involves the mistrafficking of NTB-A, which phenotypically resembles Vpu-mediated BST2 mistrafficking (Bolduan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Bolduan et al., 2013).

claim: Vpu causes retention of NTB-A in a perinuclear compartment, although degradation is not induced.
source: Although degradation is not induced, Vpu causes retention of NTB-A in a perinuclear compartment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Bolduan et al., 2013).

claim: Like BST2, the downregulation of NTB-A depends on an interaction between the transmembrane domains of Vpu and NTB-A.
source: Like BST2, the downregulation depends on an interaction between the transmembrane domains of Vpu and NTB-A (Shah et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Shah et al., 2010).

claim: Residues other than the conserved phosphorylated serines in VpuCD are critical for NTB-A downregulation.
source: In addition, residues other than the conserved phosphorylated serines in VpuCD are critical (Bolduan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Bolduan et al., 2013).

claim: Downregulation of CD1d by Vpu occurs through interference with the recycling of CD1d in the endosomal compartments.
source: In the case of CD1d, an antigen-presenting molecule in dendritic cells, downregulation by Vpu occurs through interference with the recycling of CD1d in the endosomal compartments (Moll et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Moll et al., 2010).

claim: A critical residue of CD1d, Tyr331 in a canonical sorting motif, is key for both the natural trafficking and the Vpu-mediated CD1d downregulation.
source: A critical residue of CD1d, Tyr331 in a canonical sorting motif, is key for both the natural trafficking and the Vpu-mediated CD1d downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Moll et al., 2010).

claim: The modulation of NTB-A and/or CD1d by Vpu may involve clathrin-dependent trafficking pathways.
source: Given the similarities between these systems, we speculate that the modulation of NTB-A and/or CD1d by Vpu may also involve clathrin-dependent trafficking pathways.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from similarities with BST2 antagonism.

claim: One possibility for why BST2 interacts with AP1 is that the interaction allows BST2 that is internalized from the cell surface to recycle to the plasma membrane, where it acts to trap nascent virions.
source: One possibility is that the interaction with AP1 allows BST2 that is internalized from the cell surface to recycle to the plasma membrane, where it acts to trap nascent virions.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference about potential BST2 function.

claim: Another possibility is that the BST2-AP1 interaction relates to the ability of BST2 to induce the activity of the NF-κB family of transcription factors, which could occur from an endosomal compartment that BST2 reaches via AP1-dependent trafficking.
source: Another possibility derives from the ability of BST2 to induce the activity of the NF-κB family of transcription factors (Cocka and Bates, 2012; Galao et al., 2012; Tokarev et al., 2013); this signaling function could occur from an endosomal compartment that BST2 reaches via AP1-dependent trafficking.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citations to prior work (Cocka and Bates, 2012; Galao et al., 2012; Tokarev et al., 2013) and inference.

claim: Yet another possibility is that BST2 uses AP1 to divert tethered virions to late endosomal compartments in antigen presenting cells, thus facilitating the presentation of viral antigens in the context of class II or class I MHC.
source: Yet another possibility is that BST2 uses AP1 to divert tethered virions to late endosomal compartments in antigen presenting cells, thus facilitating the presentation of viral antigens in the context of class II or class I MHC (Neil et al., 2006; Miyakawa et al., 2009; Moffat et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citations to prior work (Neil et al., 2006; Miyakawa et al., 2009; Moffat et al., 2013) and inference.
